item: plugins/house/modules/claude-code/rules/claude-code.md (headings matching hook, settings, model, subagent, peer session, git state) plus plugins/house/hooks/no-direct-master.sh

rules.heading: Keep the auto-memory index to hooks, and hold it under its cap
rules.evidence: Nothing in the MCP permissioning or headless facts governs the size or shape of the auto-memory index. The only headless fact that touches auto memory at all is coverage, not content: "--bare to reduce startup time by skipping auto-discovery of hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md", which removes the index from a run rather than capping it. The cap itself lives in the memory docs, which are outside the two areas this pass judges against.

rules.heading: Disable model invocation on a skill with side effects
rules.nativeFeature: Skills and custom commands in print mode, plus the auto permission mode's classifier review
rules.evidence: The rule builds on the frontmatter gate and adds the posture the harness has no opinion on (which effects count as side effects). Two facts sharpen it. First, the gate is not a human gate headless: "User-invoked skills and custom commands work in -p mode: include /skill-name in the prompt string and Claude Code expands it before running", so a script that writes the prompt fires the skill with nobody at a prompt. Second, the rule's classifier expectation is real and native: the auto permission mode is documented as one where "a classifier reviews most actions instead of you". The rule currently says "only a person can fire it", which overstates what the frontmatter buys in a print-mode run.
rules.proposedWording:
Set `disable-model-invocation: true` on any skill that writes, deploys, or spends, so nothing in the session can fire it on its own and its body costs nothing until a caller names it.
Remember that a print-mode run expands a skill named in the prompt string before the turn starts, so the gate is the caller who wrote that string and not a person watching a prompt.
Make the later phases of a procedure explicit opt-in gates rather than an automatic continuation.
Expect an automatic mode to route a production deploy through a classifier rather than through you, and answer that with explicit intent rather than a route around it.
Anchor: none (because frontmatter cannot tell which effects are side effects; skill review is the check).
Receipts: `docs/handbook/claude-code.md#disable-model-invocation-on-a-skill-with-side-effects`

rules.heading: Set the model explicitly on every subagent and workflow agent
rules.nativeFeature: --max-budget-usd print-mode ceiling, and the managed availableModels list exception to settings merging
rules.evidence: Model inheritance on an agent call has no counterpart in either area, so the core rule stands. Two adjacent floors it should name. The cost clause is currently prose where the harness has enforcement: "--max-budget-usd sets Maximum dollar amount to spend on API calls", listed as blocking and print-mode only. And an explicitly named tier is not always grantable: "availableModels is a separate exception: a managed availableModels list is applied as-is and non-managed entries are ignored, and it never merges across managed sources either", so a named tier can simply be absent under managed settings.
rules.proposedWording:
Name the model on every agent call, because an omitted one silently inherits the session's and a wide fan-out then runs at whatever tier you happened to be in.
Match the tier to the task: mechanical joins and receipt checks at the small tier, code and prose in the middle, judgment and adjudication at the top.
Expect a managed model list to be applied as given rather than merged with yours, so a named tier can be unavailable and the call has to fail loudly rather than quietly fall back.
State the tier a procedure requires and stop when the session is below it, and give a scripted run the print-mode budget ceiling flag so a cost constraint is enforced rather than only stated.
Anchor: the eval pair at `plugins/house/evals/explicit-model-tier/`, whose arms differ only in whether each call sets a model.
Receipts: `docs/handbook/claude-code.md#set-the-model-explicitly-on-every-subagent-and-workflow-agent`

rules.heading: Make a must-hold rule a hook, fail it closed, and test it with real payloads
rules.nativeFeature: PreToolUse hook decision mechanics and the deny-rule floor beneath them, plus the hook-skipping startup flags
rules.evidence: The fail-closed posture is exactly right and is confirmed native: "Exit code 0 with no output means the hook has no decision to report, so the tool call continues through the normal permission flow. The hook can deny the call, but staying silent doesn't approve it." The broad-matcher advice is also vindicated by a documented matcher hazard: "a bare hyphenated prefix like mcp__brave-search is evaluated as an unanchored regular expression and matches every tool from that server." What the rule misses is that a hook is not the outermost floor. Deny rules run regardless ("Claude Code evaluates deny and ask rules regardless of what a PreToolUse hook returns"), and the hook itself disappears under several startup shapes: --bare "skipping auto-discovery of hooks", --safe-mode starting "with all customizations (CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers ...) disabled", and --restricted which "ignores user, project and local settings files". So "only a pre-tool hook stops the action" is true only for sessions that load hooks.
rules.proposedWording:
Turn a rule that must hold every time into a hook, because a rule file is advisory context and only a pre-tool hook stops the action.
Know the floor under the hook: a deny rule is evaluated whatever the hook returns, and a session started bare, in safe mode, or in restricted mode never loads project hooks at all, so anything that must survive those needs a deny rule in managed settings beside it.
Fail it closed: a crash, a missing helper, or an unreadable payload denies rather than passing quietly, because a silent exit reads as no decision and never as approval, and the matcher stays broad because a matcher filter is best-effort, so the script decides.
Escalate as autonomy rises, from a prompt, to a check the agent runs before you walk away, to a hook, to a verification subagent.
Read a permission block as evidence of a wrong step earlier, not as an obstacle to route around.
Anchor: `bash tests/hooks/run.sh` drives real payloads through the real hook wiring, with a denied case, an allowed case, and a planted internal failure.
Receipts: `docs/handbook/claude-code.md#make-a-must-hold-rule-a-hook-fail-it-closed-and-test-it-with-real-payloads`

rules.heading: Run adversarial review in a fresh subagent with a named lens
rules.nativeFeature: --forward-subagent-text / CLAUDE_CODE_FORWARD_SUBAGENT_TEXT, and the print-mode background-subagent wait ceiling
rules.evidence: The named lens and the flag-only-correctness instruction have no native counterpart, so the rule is additive. Its recovery clause rides on a real primitive: by default only subagent tool_use and tool_result blocks reach the stream, and the flag "also emits subagent text and thinking blocks as assistant/user messages carrying parent_tool_use_id, letting you reconstruct each subagent's transcript", forwarding "messages from subagents at every nesting depth". The killed-fan-out case is also bounded natively: a print-mode run waits for background subagents "capped ... at ten minutes of continuous idle waiting by default, adjustable via CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS". Nothing here contradicts the rule; the transcript-recovery advice simply presumes a stream the flag is what produces.

rules.heading: Treat git state as shared across sessions
rules.nativeFeature: Background session subcommands (claude --bg, attach, stop/kill, rm, respawn) and print-mode SIGTERM behavior
rules.evidence: The harness supplies the concurrency this rule is defending against and none of the defense. Background sessions are first class ("claude --bg/--background starts a session in the background and returns immediately", "claude rm <id> deletes it (and its worktree when safe)"), which is precisely the other checkout that can move a branch mid-run. The stranded-work risk is documented rather than prevented: on SIGTERM a print run "leaves the turn that was in progress unfinished and records no result for it" and "terminates the process tree of any still-running Bash command". No native mechanism asks before switching, prefers a worktree, or re-reads the branch before a commit, so the rule and its hook anchor add enforcement the harness lacks.

rules.heading: Keep the committed settings narrow and the local settings local
rules.nativeFeature: Permission list merging across scopes, MCP allow/deny wildcard asymmetry, the settings-file skip of parameter-scoped MCP rules, and headless loading of project MCP servers without approval
rules.evidence: Four facts sharpen this rule, none contradict it. The prune clause is now mechanically justified: "When you set the same list key, such as permissions.allow, in more than one file, Claude Code combines the lists instead of picking one", so a broad grant anywhere really does outrank every narrow one. The blanket advice needs a side: "Deny and ask rules also accept glob patterns in the tool-name position ... mcp__* matches every MCP tool across all servers", while "Allow rules accept tool-name globs only after a literal mcp__<server>__ prefix ... An unanchored allow glob ... is skipped with a warning". A narrowing attempt can silently vanish: "When Claude Code loads a settings file, it skips any mcp__ rule that has parentheses." And pinning servers matters most exactly where nobody is watching: "In non-interactive modes (claude -p, Agent SDK, cloud sessions): Claude Code can't show that prompt: it loads project-scoped servers without asking."
rules.proposedWording:
Commit an allowlist covering the repo's own script surface and read-side platform commands and nothing broader, and authorize deploy and egress verbs through a skill instead.
Allow-list network fetches per domain rather than blanket, and pin the servers and services the project enables by name rather than inheriting whatever is installed, because a print-mode run loads the project's servers with no approval prompt at all.
Reach for a deny rule when you want the blanket, since a deny can wildcard across every tool of every server while an allow has to name its server, and keep a parameter-scoped rule on a server tool out of a settings file, because the loader skips it and says so only in the doctor output.
Keep the wide accreted list in `settings.local.json`, gitignored and free of machine paths, and forward-declare a script you are about to add so its first run needs no prompt.
Prune it on a cadence, because permission lists merge across every scope rather than override, so one broad grant supersedes every careful narrow one and a stale entry outlives the rename that orphaned it.
Anchor: `plugins/house/templates/settings.json` ships the narrow committed allowlist with no hooks block, and `/house-rules:sync` refuses a managed file that was edited locally.
Receipts: `docs/handbook/claude-code.md#keep-the-committed-settings-narrow-and-the-local-settings-local`

rules.heading: Check for a peer session before driving shared external state
rules.nativeFeature: Background session subcommands, specifically claude agents as the listing primitive
rules.evidence: The listing step the rule opens with is a real native command ("claude agents lists them", alongside attach, logs, stop, kill, rm, respawn), but the harness stops at enumeration: nothing in either area arbitrates ownership of a shared application, database, or checkout, and nothing prevents a deploy from a checkout another session occupies. The rule adds the posture and the deploy-guard enforcement on top of a listing the harness already provides.

rules.heading: PreToolUse branch guard
rules.nativeFeature: PreToolUse hook decision mechanics, the Cowork mcp__workspace__bash routing of shell commands, and hook-skipping startup flags
rules.evidence: The script's mechanics match the documented contract exactly: it emits permissionDecision deny and exits zero rather than exiting non-zero, which is right because "Exit code 0 with no output means the hook has no decision to report" and a silent exit "doesn't approve it"; its jq-missing and crash paths are the only ways it produces a decision without evidence, and both deny. Its blind spots come from the new areas. It reads .tool_input.command and only ever guards Bash-shaped payloads, but "In a Cowork session in the Claude Desktop app, Claude runs shell commands through Cowork's mcp__workspace__bash tool rather than the built-in Bash tool", and any git operation performed by an MCP server arrives as mcp__server__tool instead, so neither reaches this guard. Where that matters, the surviving floor is a deny rule naming the whole tool, since "Claude Code also applies deny rules that name the whole Bash or WebFetch tool to these Cowork tools" while "Allow rules don't carry over". The guard also disappears entirely from a session started with --bare or --safe-mode, and from --restricted, which "ignores user, project and local settings files".
rules.proposedWording:
Add to the fail-open documentation block at the top of the script:
# Also fails open, silently, wherever this hook never runs or never sees the
# command: a session started bare or in safe mode loads no project hooks,
# restricted mode ignores project settings, and a shell command routed
# through a Cowork workspace tool or a git operation performed by an MCP
# server arrives as an MCP tool call rather than a Bash one, so nothing here
# inspects it. Where that coverage matters, a deny rule naming the whole tool
# is the only floor that still binds; an allow rule for Bash never carries
# over to the Cowork tool.

notes:
Scope calls: I selected headings by the literal keyword list (hook, settings, model, subagent, peer session, git state), which yields eight rule headings plus the branch guard. That excludes "Don't", whose bullets restate several in-scope rules (hook matcher scoping, model inheritance, allowlist width) and would draw the same dispositions; if the owner wants the Don't list judged, it should be a separate entry rather than inherited.

I judged strictly against the MCP-permissioning and headless fact sets as instructed, and deliberately did not use the third bundled fact set (output styles, plan mode, CLAUDE.md and rules loading). That matters most for "Keep the auto-memory index to hooks, and hold it under its cap", which I marked UNIQUE: the memory-area facts do carry an auto-memory index load cap that would likely make it a DUPLICATE-or-COMPLEMENT call, so that heading should be re-judged in the pass that owns those facts before anyone concludes it has no native counterpart.

Two things I could not verify from the given facts. First, the exact payload shape a Cowork mcp__workspace__bash call presents to a PreToolUse hook: the facts establish that shell commands route through that MCP tool and that Bash deny rules reach it, but not whether a hook matcher and a .tool_input.command field see anything usable. My branch-guard finding assumes they do not, which is the conservative reading; if the field is present, the gap narrows to non-Cowork MCP git servers only. Second, whether a permissionDecision deny in JSON is treated as absolute in the same way exit code two is: the facts state exit two "does take precedence over allow rules" and that a blocking hook is absolute, but they only describe the JSON deny form as one of the outputs, so I did not claim equivalence in the proposed wording.

For "Set the model explicitly on every subagent and workflow agent" the managed availableModels point is inferred one step: the fact states a managed list is applied as-is with non-managed entries ignored, and I read that as meaning a named tier can be unavailable. The facts do not say what happens to an agent call that names an unavailable model, so the proposed line says the call must fail loudly rather than asserting that it does.
